title: MZ Failed To Initialize Graphics (only with a Plugin)

posts.author: lordvalinar
posts.body:
I require the help of the community to understand what's going on and maybe how to fix this...
1.) Backed up my RMMZ projects (Documents folder)
2.) Built new PC
3.) Installed Steam
4.) Installed RPG Maker MZ
5.) Put RMMZ projects back in Documents
6.) Loaded up a project -> Working on plugin
When I playtest I get "Failed to initialize graphics". When I disable the plugin, it works just fine. I am a bit confused by this as the console doesn't lead to anywhere near my plugin, nor mentions it, and nothing my plugin does touches the manager functions ... (Well DataManager.loadDatabase - but I commented that section out when I continued to test the error).
Any ideas? I've tried copying over the "img" folder from "newproject" in the actual MZ folder to my project folder and still nothing. I have latest drivers on everything (chipset, gpu, etc). Definitely not a PC issue.

posts.author: ShadowDragon
posts.body:
it may be because your browser has unsupported WebGL or is disabled.
if its disabled, turn it on, if its unsupported, this may be your issue.

so far I know, MZ heavily rely on PIXI v5 which can't render if something happens.
so I would check your browser or security if its blocks something in order to render.
but thats all I can see from the rmmz manager.

posts.author: caethyril
posts.body:
With no plugins, that error means that
Graphics.initialize
did not return truthy, i.e. the PIXI app,
Graphics._app
, was not created for some reason.
A plugin could reliably cause your error trace by altering a relevant method of
Graphics
, e.g.
JavaScript:
Graphics._createPixiApp = function() { /** do nothing */ };

posts.author: lordvalinar
caethyril
posts.body:
Object.keys
returns all enumerable keys, and you have added the
matches
function as a new enumerable key.
Functions are of type
object
, hence I believe this part of your original code would recurse until it errors out due to maximum call depth:
lordvalinar said:
JavaScript:
return (typeof this[key] === "object" && typeof obj[key] === "object")
            ? this[key].matches(obj[key])
            : this[key] === obj[key];
Click to expand...
[Edit: as Solar_Flare points out, I misremembered:
typeof
actually returns
function
for functions. So the actual problem may well be something else.]
Object.defineProperty
defaults to
enumerable: false
, so you could probably have used that instead. Like Aerosys said, though, I think I'd personally use a different approach.

posts.author: Aerosys
caethyril
posts.body:
lordvalinar said:
Well I have the Array.prototype.matches set to false, I don't know if that would have affected the Object.prototype.matches?
Click to expand...
No. I'm not sure why you would think that. You've defined the property on both prototypes, so they're mutually independent rather than one inheriting from the other. Even so,
Array
inherits from
Object
, not the other way around.
I strongly recommend rearranging your code like Aerosys suggested!
Regardless, I think it would be a good idea for you to (re)learn about inheritance in object-oriented programming, since it's a very important concept. E.g.
Inheritance and the prototype chain - JavaScript | MDN
In programming, inheritance refers to passing down characteristics from a parent to a child so that a new piece of code can reuse and build upon the features of an existing one. JavaScript implements inheritance by using objects. Each object has an internal link to another object called its...

Generally speaking, I don't agree with Aerosys and caethyril that you shouldn't ever add functions to the
Array
prototype (or even the
Object
prototype), but you should definitely never add
enumerable
properties to them (always use
defineProperty
or
defineProperties
with
enumerable: false
). Still, since it was somehow causing problems in this case and you couldn't figure out how, just making it a standalone function is probably the best option.

Aerosys
posts.body:
Don't try to reinvent the wheel. It's not a shame to copy-paste from StackOverflow
(well, not always)
.
I think this one is a good candidate, it's not the top-voted answer, but it's much easier to read:
https://stackoverflow.com/a/45683145
Again, especially for beginners, it's probably easier to compare by fixed attributes instead of "everything". Usually, you know what your objects and lists contain, e.g. it's a list of actors, then you can compare by IDs or names. This gives you more control than a magix function that still hasn't covered edge-cases (e.g. NaN == NaN actually returns false).
